title: Anatolia
subtitle: 1908–1923 · Revolution, the Great War, the Destruction of the Christian Communities and the National Struggle

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The last sultans, the Young Turk cabinets and triumvirate, the armistice governments and the Ankara assembly

entries.label: Abdülhamid II restored to a constitution
entries.hint: Under the pressure of the revolution in Macedonia, Abdülhamid II announced the restoration of the constitution on 24 July 1908 and reopened parliament. After the counter-revolt of April 1909 was put down by the Action Army, parliament voted to depose him on 27 April 1909 and sent him to Salonica. His brother Mehmed V was put on the throne.
entries.note: Irade of 23–24 July 1908; deposition fetva and parliamentary resolution, 27 April 1909; Feroz Ahmad, The Young Turks (1969); Sina Akşin, Jön Türkler ve İttihat ve Terakki (1980).

entries.label: Mehmed V Reşad
entries.hint: Mehmed V, sultan and caliph from 1909 to 1918, was a constitutional figurehead and left government to the cabinets and, behind them, to the Committee of Union and Progress. He proclaimed the jihad in November 1914. He died in July 1918, a few months before the armistice.
entries.note: Kanun-ı Esasi, as amended August 1909; Erik Zürcher, Turkey: A Modern History (1993); Caroline Finkel, Osman's Dream (2005).

entries.label: Mehmed VI Vahdeddin
entries.hint: Mehmed VI succeeded his brother in July 1918, dissolved parliament in April 1920 and, under the occupation of Istanbul, kept governments that were ready to accept the Allies' terms. The nationalists treated him as a captive of the occupiers, and when the Ankara assembly abolished the sultanate on 1 November 1922, he left Istanbul on a British warship on 17 November.
entries.note: GNA resolution of 1 November 1922; Zürcher 1993; Finkel 2005.

entries.label: Abdülmecid II as caliph
entries.hint: After the sultanate was abolished, the Grand National Assembly on 18 November 1922 elected Abdülmecid, a prince of the house of Osman, as caliph, a religious office without temporal power. He lived in Istanbul under the eye of the Ankara government until the caliphate itself was abolished in March 1924.
entries.note: GNA resolution of 18 November 1922; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: Mustafa Kemal elected first president
entries.hint: On 29 October 1923 the assembly amended the Law of Fundamental Organisation to declare Turkey a republic, and elected Mustafa Kemal its first president. He was re-elected until his death in 1938. İsmet İnönü was named prime minister the following day.
entries.note: Law no. 364 (29 October 1923); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The cabinets of the revolution
entries.hint: A succession of grand viziers (Kâmil Pasha, Hüseyin Hilmi, Hakkı Pasha, Ahmed Muhtar and others) governed under the restored constitution, while the Committee of Union and Progress kept a hand on them from behind the parliament. The party's rivals, the Liberal Union, held the government in the summer and autumn of 1912, before the CUP regained it by the coup of January 1913.
entries.note: Feroz Ahmad 1969; Zürcher 1993; Erik Zürcher, The Young Turk Legacy (2010).

entries.label: The triumvirate: Talat, Enver and Cemal
entries.hint: On 23 January 1913 Enver and a group of CUP officers stormed the Sublime Porte and forced the cabinet to resign. From then until October 1918 power lay with Talat Pasha (interior minister and, from 1917, grand vizier), Enver Pasha (war minister) and Cemal Pasha (navy minister and commander in Syria). They took the empire into the Great War, and the three are held responsible for the deportations of 1915.
entries.note: Raid on the Sublime Porte (23 January 1913); Hasan Kayalı, Arabs and Young Turks (1997); Taner Akçam, A Shameful Act (2006).

entries.label: The armistice governments
entries.hint: After the CUP leaders fled in November 1918, grand viziers Ahmed İzzet, Tevfik Pasha, Damat Ferid Pasha and Ali Rıza Pasha formed a succession of cabinets under the eyes of the Allies. Damat Ferid's governments were hostile to the CUP and to the nationalists; Ali Rıza's allowed contacts with the national movement.
entries.note: Zürcher 1993; Finkel 2005; Ottoman cabinet lists (Düstur).

entries.label: Mustafa Kemal and the Representative Committee
entries.hint: Mustafa Kemal, an Ottoman general who had gone to Samsun in May 1919 as inspector for the army in the east, resigned his commission in July and was elected head of the Representative Committee of the congresses of Erzurum and Sivas. The committee acted as the leadership of the national movement from the end of 1919, when it moved to Ankara.
entries.note: Erzurum Congress (23 July–7 August 1919); Sivas Congress (4–11 September 1919); Nutuk (1927); Zürcher, The Unionist Factor (1984).

entries.label: The Grand National Assembly
entries.hint: The Grand National Assembly opened at Ankara on 23 April 1920, with deputies from the last Ottoman parliament who had escaped and with members elected in the provinces, and chose Mustafa Kemal as its president. It combined legislative and executive power, ruled through a council of ministers it elected, and from 1921 had its own constitution.
entries.note: GNA minutes (TBMM Zabıt Ceridesi), 23 April 1920; Teşkilât-ı Esasiye Kanunu (1921); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The Ankara cabinets
entries.hint: The councils of ministers elected by the assembly were led by Fevzi (Çakmak) from 1920 to 1922, then by Rauf (Orbay) in 1922–1923, and briefly by Fethi (Okyar) in 1923. Mustafa Kemal chaired the assembly. After the Republic, İsmet became prime minister.
entries.note: TBMM records; Zürcher 1993.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The revolution and the Adana massacres, the Balkan wars, the Great War fronts, the deportation and killing of the Armenians, Assyrians and Greeks, and the Greco-Turkish war

entries.label: The Young Turk revolution
entries.hint: Officers of the Third Army in Macedonia, led by Niyazi of Resne and Enver, went to the hills in July 1908 in the name of the 1876 constitution, and the sultan yielded on 24 July. The revolution was welcomed in the Anatolian provinces as the end of tyranny, and Muslims, Armenians and Greeks celebrated it in the streets.
entries.note: Şükrü Hanioğlu, The Young Turks in Opposition (1995) and Preparation for a Revolution (2001); Feroz Ahmad 1969.

entries.label: The Adana massacres
entries.hint: In April 1909, during the counter-revolt in Istanbul, mobs and soldiers attacked the Armenians of Adana and the villages of Cilicia in two waves, on 14–17 April and again on 25–27 April, burning their quarters. Estimates of the Armenian dead run from about 15,000 to 30,000, with the Ottoman government's own count far lower. A parliamentary commission was sent and courts-martial hanged a number of Muslims and some Armenians, but the victims' hopes of justice were not met.
entries.note: Ottoman parliamentary commission report (1909); Bedross Der Matossian, The Horrors of Adana (2022); Robert Tatoyan, International Journal of Armenian Genocide Studies (2024).

entries.label: The Balkan Wars
entries.hint: The Balkan League of Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro attacked the empire in October 1912 and in a few weeks took nearly all of its European provinces. Edirne fell in March 1913 and was recovered by Enver in July. The war sent hundreds of thousands of Muslim refugees into Anatolia and Thrace and deepened the suspicion of many in the Muslim elite towards the empire's Christian subjects.
entries.note: Treaty of London (30 May 1913); Treaty of Constantinople (29 September 1913); Erik Zürcher, 'Greek and Turkish refugees and deportees 1912–1924' (2003); Hall, The Balkan Wars (2000).

entries.label: The persecution of the Ottoman Greeks
entries.hint: From 1913–1914 the Ottoman government drove Greek communities from the Aegean coast and Thrace, as at Phocaea in June 1914, and conscripted Greek men into labour battalions in which many died. In the Pontus in 1916–1923 deportations and killings continued under the CUP and under the nationalist Independence Tribunals. Estimates of the Ottoman Greek dead run from about 300,000 to 900,000; the Greek parliament (1994, 1998), the IAGS (2007) and some other bodies call these events genocide, and the Turkish state disputes the term and points to the violence of the Greek occupation of 1919–1922.
entries.note: Matthias Bjørnlund, 'The 1914 cleansing of Aegean Greeks' (2008); Tessa Hofmann (ed.), The Genocide of the Ottoman Greeks (2011); Zürcher 2003; Greek Law 2193/1994.

entries.label: Sarıkamış
entries.hint: In December 1914 Enver took personal command of the Third Army on the Caucasus front and launched a winter offensive around the Russian position at Sarıkamış. In the deep snow and cold the army was shattered by frost, typhus and Russian counter-attack; of about 90,000 men, most were lost. The defeat left eastern Anatolia open to the Russians.
entries.note: Edward Erickson, Ordered to Die (2001); Allen and Muratoff, Caucasian Battlefields (1953); Ottoman General Staff, Birinci Dünya Harbi.

entries.label: The Sayfo
entries.hint: The Assyrian, Chaldean and Syriac Christians of Hakkâri, Siirt and Tur Abdin were attacked in 1915 by Ottoman troops, Kurdish tribal forces and local Muslim neighbours, and were killed or driven out. The Syriac name for the events is Sayfo, 'the sword'. Estimates of the dead run from about 150,000 to 300,000, perhaps half of the community; several parliaments and the IAGS (2007) have called these events genocide, and the Turkish state rejects the term.
entries.note: David Gaunt, Massacres, Resistance, Protectors (2006); Hannibal Travis, Genocide in the Middle East (2010); IAGS resolution (December 2007).

entries.label: Gallipoli
entries.hint: After the Allied fleet failed to force the Dardanelles on 18 March 1915, British, French and Anzac troops landed on the Gallipoli peninsula on 25 April. Ottoman divisions under Mustafa Kemal, Esat Pasha and the German Liman von Sanders held the heights through months of trench warfare, and the Allies evacuated in December 1915 and January 1916. It was the empire's greatest military victory in the war, and a founding story of the Republic.
entries.note: Robin Prior, Gallipoli: The End of the Myth (2009); Erickson, Gallipoli (2015); Turkish General Staff, Çanakkale Cephesi Harekâtı.

entries.label: The Armenian Genocide
entries.hint: From April 1915 the Ottoman government arrested the Armenian elite of Istanbul and deported the Armenians of the eastern provinces and then most of Anatolia to the Syrian desert; men were separated and killed, and the convoys of women, children and old people died of massacre, hunger and disease or were absorbed into Muslim households. Estimates of the dead run from about 600,000 to 1.5 million, most scholars putting it near a million. The great majority of genocide scholars, the International Association of Genocide Scholars (1997) and the Allied declaration of 24 May 1915 ('crimes against humanity and civilisation') treat the events as a crime of this order, and Ottoman courts-martial in 1919–1920 convicted CUP leaders of organising massacres. The Republic of Turkey rejects the term genocide, calls the deportation a wartime relocation made necessary by revolutionary activity and collaboration with Russia, and attributes the deaths to disease, famine and inter-communal violence. As of 2026 governments remain divided.
entries.note: Allied joint declaration (24 May 1915); Takvim-i Vekayi no. 3540–3771 (1919–1920, trials); Taner Akçam, A Shameful Act (2006); Ronald Suny, They Can Live in the Desert but Nowhere Else (2015); Raymond Kévorkian, The Armenian Genocide (2011); Turkish Historical Society (Türk Tarih Kurumu) publications for the official position; IAGS resolution (1997).

entries.label: The arrests of 24 April 1915
entries.hint: On the night of 24 April 1915, on the eve of the Gallipoli landing, police arrested some 250 Armenian community leaders, writers, doctors and deputies in Istanbul and sent most of them to camps near Ankara; the majority were later killed. The date is commemorated every year as the day of remembrance of the genocide.
entries.note: Ottoman interior ministry order (24 April 1915); Akçam 2006; Kévorkian 2011; Peter Balakian, The Burning Tigris (2003).

entries.label: The defence of Van
entries.hint: In April 1915 the Armenians of Van, after fighting with the governor Cevdet Bey's forces and under siege, held the city quarters until the Russian army arrived in mid-May. The Ottoman state has presented the rising as proof of Armenian treason; Armenian and many other historians see it as a defence against deportation and killing already begun in the province. Thousands of Muslim civilians also died in the fighting and flight, and when the Russians withdrew in July the Armenians left with them.
entries.note: Kévorkian 2011; Justin McCarthy, The Armenian Rebellion at Van (2006); Suny 2015.

entries.label: The Russian occupation of eastern Anatolia
entries.hint: The Russians, with Armenian volunteer units attached, took Erzurum in February 1916, Trabzon in April and Erzincan in July, and held a large part of eastern Anatolia until the army dissolved after the Revolution of 1917. In 1918 the Ottoman Third Army retook Erzurum, Kars and the border districts, and the Muslim population returned to what was left. The fighting left a wasteland.
entries.note: Allen and Muratoff 1953; Richard Hovannisian, The Republic of Armenia (1971–96).

entries.label: The Greek landing at Smyrna
entries.hint: Greek troops, authorised by the Allied leaders in Paris, landed at Izmir on 15 May 1919 amid the cheers of the Greek population; shots were fired on the quay as they marched in, and Turks were killed in the first days. An Allied commission of inquiry later found that the Greek occupation had been marked by violence against Muslims. The landing set off the resistance movement in western Anatolia.
entries.note: Report of the Inter-Allied Commission of Inquiry (October 1919); Michael Llewellyn Smith, Ionian Vision (1973); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The southern front: Maraş, Antep and Urfa
entries.hint: After the French took over Cilicia from the British in late 1919, the towns of Maraş, Antep and Urfa rose against their garrisons. Maraş fought the French and Armenian Legion in February 1920; Antep resisted a long siege from April 1920 to February 1921. The Armenians of Maraş and Urfa suffered in the fighting and its aftermath, and thousands left with the French. Under the Franklin-Bouillon agreement of October 1921 the French withdrew from Cilicia.
entries.note: Franklin-Bouillon–Fethi agreement (20 October 1921); Stanford Shaw, From Empire to Republic (2000); Kévorkian 2011.

entries.label: The eastern front and the Republic of Armenia
entries.hint: In September 1920 Kâzım Karabekir's army attacked the Republic of Armenia, took Kars in October and pushed on to Gümrü, where an armistice and on 2–3 December the treaty of Alexandropol ended the war. The Armenian republic, already ruined by famine and refugees, gave up Kars and Ardahan and gave way to Soviet rule within days. There were reports of killings of Armenian civilians in the districts the Turkish army took.
entries.note: Treaty of Alexandropol (2–3 December 1920); Hovannisian 1971–96; Karabekir, İstiklâl Harbimiz (1960).

entries.label: The Koçgiri rebellion
entries.hint: In 1920 Alevi Kurdish tribes of the Koçgiri district rose against the Ankara government, in part in the name of Kurdish autonomy as promised by the Sèvres treaty, and were put down with heavy loss by Ankara's forces by the middle of 1921. The assembly's Kurdish deputies debated the matter. It was an early Kurdish revolt against the Ankara government.
entries.note: TBMM secret sessions (1921); Martin van Bruinessen, Agha, Shaikh and State (1992); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: Sakarya
entries.hint: In the summer of 1921 the Greek army advanced from Eskişehir towards Ankara and in twenty-two days of fighting on the Sakarya, about 80 km from the capital, was stopped by the Turkish army under Mustafa Kemal and İsmet. The Greek army withdrew to its lines. The assembly gave Mustafa Kemal the rank of marshal and the title of gazi.
entries.note: Turkish General Staff, Türk İstiklal Harbi; Llewellyn Smith 1973; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The Great Offensive and Dumlupınar
entries.hint: The Turkish offensive began on 26 August 1922 at Afyon, broke the Greek front in a day and encircled the main Greek force at Dumlupınar on 30 August. The Greek army fell back to the coast in disorder, burning villages and towns on its way. Turkish cavalry entered Izmir on 9 September.
entries.note: Türk İstiklal Harbi; Llewellyn Smith 1973; Inter-Allied report on Greek retreat (1922).

entries.label: The burning of Smyrna
entries.hint: A fire that began on 13 September 1922, four days after the Turkish army entered Izmir, destroyed the Armenian and Greek quarters of the city and left the Turkish and Jewish quarters standing. Tens of thousands of refugees crowded the quay to be taken off by Allied warships. Estimates of the dead range from about 10,000 to 100,000; who set the fire is disputed, Turkish accounts blaming Greek and Armenian arsonists and most Greek, Armenian and western eyewitnesses blaming Turkish soldiers.
entries.note: George Horton, The Blight of Asia (1926); Marjorie Housepian Dobkin, Smyrna 1922 (1971); Giles Milton, Paradise Lost (2008); Turkish official accounts.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The restored constitution, the deportation law, the courts-martial of 1919–1920, Sèvres, the National Pact, the end of the sultanate and Lausanne

entries.label: The restored constitution and its amendment
entries.hint: In August 1909 parliament amended the constitution of 1876 so as to raise the power of the chamber and the cabinet and to limit the sultan's prerogatives: ministers became responsible to the chamber, and the sultan lost the power to exile subjects at will. The change gave the empire a constitutional monarchy on paper.
entries.note: Kanun-ı Esasi, amended August 1909 (Düstur); Feroz Ahmad 1969.

entries.label: The Armenian reform agreement
entries.hint: Under Russian and German pressure the Ottoman government signed an agreement on 8 February 1914 to place the six eastern provinces with large Armenian populations under two foreign inspectors-general, the Dutchman Louis Westenenk and the Norwegian Nicolai Hoff. They arrived in Istanbul in 1914 and were sent home when the war began.
entries.note: Reform agreement of 8 February 1914; Roderic Davison, 'The Armenian Crisis, 1912–1914' (1948); Hovannisian 1997.

entries.label: The deportation law and the abandoned property laws
entries.hint: A provisional law of 27 May 1915 authorised the army to deport the inhabitants of villages and towns suspected of espionage or treason, and in the autumn of 1915 further decrees put the property left behind into the care of liquidation commissions. In practice the laws were applied against the Armenians. The law was published in the official gazette on 1 June.
entries.note: Geçici Kanun (27 May 1915; Takvim-i Vekayi 1 June 1915); Emval-i Metruke regulations (September–November 1915); Akçam 2006; Üngör and Polatel, Confiscation and Destruction (2011).

entries.label: The Ottoman family law
entries.hint: The Hukuk-ı Aile Kararnamesi of 25 October 1917 was the first codification of Ottoman family law, drawing on several schools of Islamic law and giving women some stipulations in the marriage contract and grounds for divorce, while leaving polygamy in place. It was suspended in 1919 and revoked soon after.
entries.note: Hukuk-ı Aile Kararnamesi (25 October 1917, Düstur); Zürcher 1993; Deniz Kandiyoti (ed.), Women, Islam and the State (1991).

entries.label: The armistice of Mudros
entries.hint: The Ottoman delegation signed the armistice of Mudros with the British on the battleship Agamemnon on 30 October 1918. It required demobilisation, the opening of the Straits and the right of the Allies to occupy any place where order was threatened; British, French and Italian troops entered the empire's territory in the following months.
entries.note: Armistice of Mudros (30 October 1918); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The courts-martial of 1919–1920
entries.hint: Under Allied pressure, the Ottoman government of Damat Ferid set up special military tribunals in 1919 to try the officials responsible for the deportations and massacres. Talat, Enver, Cemal and others, who were abroad, were sentenced to death in absentia in July 1919, and a few lesser officials, among them the district governor of Boğazlıyan, were hanged. The trials faded in 1920 as the British deported suspects to Malta and the nationalist movement took power; the Malta prisoners were exchanged for British hostages in 1921, and the verdicts were later annulled.
entries.note: Takvim-i Vekayi, 1919–1920 (indictments and verdicts); Vahakn Dadrian and Taner Akçam, Judgment at Istanbul (2011).

entries.label: The Treaty of Sèvres
entries.hint: The treaty signed by the Istanbul government gave the Greeks Izmir and Eastern Thrace, an Armenian state in the northeast, a Kurdish autonomous area in the east and zones to Italy and France, and put the Straits and the empire's finances under foreign control. The Ankara assembly rejected it, and it was never ratified.
entries.note: Treaty of Sèvres (10 August 1920); Zürcher 1993; Shaw 2000.

entries.label: The National Pact
entries.hint: The last Ottoman parliament, meeting in Istanbul, adopted on 28 January 1920 the Misak-ı Millî, or National Pact, which declared the regions with a Muslim majority an indivisible whole and demanded independence, the abolition of capitulations and a plebiscite in some provinces. Britain occupied Istanbul on 16 March and arrested deputies.
entries.note: Misak-ı Millî (28 January 1920); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The Law of Fundamental Organisation
entries.hint: The Ankara assembly adopted on 20 January 1921 the Teşkilât-ı Esasiye Kanunu, a short constitution proclaiming that sovereignty belongs without conditions to the nation, and that the assembly exercises it through its own executive. It became the basis of the new state.
entries.note: Teşkilât-ı Esasiye Kanunu (no. 85, 20 January 1921); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The abolition of the sultanate
entries.hint: After the victory of August–September 1922, the assembly on 1 November separated the sultanate from the caliphate, declared the first abolished and decreed that the form of government in Istanbul based on personal rule had passed into history from 16 March 1920. The rule of the house of Osman, of some six hundred years, ended; the caliphate was kept for sixteen months.
entries.note: GNA law no. 308 (1 November 1922); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The Treaty of Lausanne
entries.hint: After nine months of negotiation led for Turkey by İsmet, the Treaty of Lausanne of 24 July 1923 recognised the borders of Turkey in Anatolia and Eastern Thrace, ended the capitulations, put the Straits under a demilitarised regime and said nothing of an Armenian homeland or Kurdish autonomy. A separate amnesty declaration covered the offences of 1914–1922.
entries.note: Treaty of Lausanne (24 July 1923), with the Declaration of Amnesty; Zürcher 1993; Shaw 2000.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The jihad declaration, the rival fatwas of 1920, the Bektashi lodge at Hacıbektaş and the churches of the dispossessed

entries.label: The jihad declaration
entries.hint: Five fetvas of the Şeyhülislam Ürgüplü Hayri, announced at the Fatih mosque on 14 November 1914 and issued in the name of the caliph-sultan, called on Muslims everywhere to take up arms against the Allied powers. The appeal produced no rising in the British and French empires, and its effect inside the empire is debated.
entries.note: Fetva of 11 November, proclaimed 14 November 1914 (Takvim-i Vekayi); Tilman Lüdke, Jihad Made in Germany (2005); Mustafa Aksakal, The Ottoman Road to War in 1914 (2008).

entries.label: The Christian churches of Anatolia after 1915
entries.hint: With the deportation and flight of the Armenian, Greek and Syriac communities, their churches, monasteries and schools were abandoned, and many were later converted to mosques, barracks or stores, or demolished; few remained in use. The Greek Orthodox Patriarchate and the Armenian Patriarchate of Constantinople survived in Istanbul with much-reduced flocks.
entries.note: Patriarchal registers; Üngör and Polatel 2011; Kévorkian 2011.

entries.label: The Bektashi lodge at Hacıbektaş
entries.hint: Mustafa Kemal and the Representative Committee stopped on the way to Ankara at the Hacıbektaş lodge, the centre of the Bektashi order, where Cemalettin Çelebi, its head, received them in December 1919. The Bektashis and many of the Alevi villagers of central Anatolia supported the national movement.
entries.note: Nutuk (1927); Markus Dressler, Writing Religion (2013); Zürcher 1984.

entries.label: The rival fatwas of 1920
entries.hint: In April 1920 the Şeyhülislam Dürrizade Abdullah in Istanbul issued a fetva that the nationalist movement was rebellion against the caliph and that its members could be killed. The müftü of Ankara, Rıfat Börekçi, and, according to the nationalist sources, some hundreds of other müftüs answered with a fetva that the caliph was a prisoner of the infidels and it was a religious duty to resist.
entries.note: Fetva of Dürrizade Abdullah (11 April 1920); Ankara Müftüsü fetva (April 1920); Zürcher 1993.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The national anthem, the Armenian writers of 1915, the first film and the First National Style

entries.label: The First National Style
entries.hint: Architects such as Vedat Tek and Kemaleddin Bey developed in these years a 'national' style, using the forms of classical Ottoman architecture (eaves, arches, tile) for modern buildings such as post offices, offices, schools and mosques. After 1920 the style was used for the first public buildings of Ankara.
entries.note: Sibel Bozdoğan, Modernism and Nation Building (2001); Doğan Kuban, Osmanlı Mimarisi.

entries.label: The first Ottoman film
entries.hint: The army officer Fuat Uzkınay filmed in November 1914 the demolition of the Russian monument at San Stefano on the outskirts of Istanbul, the first film by a Turk according to tradition. The film was made for the army's cinema section, and is lost; the date and the first screening are disputed.
entries.note: Turkish film historiography (Nijat Özön, Türk Sineması Kronolojisi, 1960); Giovanni Scognamillo, Türk Sinema Tarihi.

entries.label: The Armenian writers of 1915
entries.hint: The Armenian poets and writers arrested in April 1915, among them Daniel Varoujan, Siamanto and Krikor Zohrab, were murdered in the summer of 1915 by gendarmes and brigands, on the roads to the interior. Komitas, the musician and priest, was spared by intervention but broke down mentally and spent his last twenty years in hospitals. The generation of Western Armenian letters was destroyed.
entries.note: Peter Balakian, The Burning Tigris (2003); Rita Soulahian Kuyumjian, Archeology of Madness (2001); Kévorkian 2011.

entries.label: The Independence March
entries.hint: The Grand National Assembly adopted on 12 March 1921 the poem of Mehmet Akif Ersoy, a poet of the Islamist school who had joined the national movement, as the national anthem, the İstiklal Marşı, from a competition in which scores of poems had been entered. The anthem, which Akif dedicated to the Turkish army, is the anthem of the Republic.
entries.note: GNA resolution (12 March 1921); Mehmet Akif Ersoy, Safahat (1911–1933).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Turkism, the debate on Ottomanism, Islamism and Turkism, and the testimony of the survivors and witnesses

entries.label: Ziya Gökalp and Turkism
entries.hint: Ziya Gökalp, a sociologist from Diyarbakır who became the ideologue of the CUP, argued that the Turks were a nation with a language, a folk culture and a civilisation of their own, distinct from the Ottoman and Islamic frames, and that the state should be built on it. His essays, 'Türkleşmek, İslâmlaşmak, Muasırlaşmak' (1918) and 'Türkçülüğün Esasları' (1923), shaped the republican ideology.
entries.note: Ziya Gökalp, Türkleşmek, İslamlaşmak, Muasırlaşmak (1918) and Türkçülüğün Esasları (1923); Uriel Heyd, Foundations of Turkish Nationalism (1950).

entries.label: Ottomanism, Islamism and Turkism
entries.hint: Between 1908 and the end of the war, the press argued over three answers to the empire's crisis: Ottomanism, a common citizenship of all subjects; Islamism, unity under the caliphate; and Turkism. As the empire lost its Christian and then its Arab provinces, the first lost ground to the other two. The debates were conducted in the journals Türk Yurdu, Sırat-ı Müstakim and İctihad.
entries.note: Yusuf Akçura, Üç Tarz-ı Siyaset (1904); Türk Yurdu (1911–); François Georgeon, Aux origines du nationalisme turc (1980).

entries.label: The documentation of 1915
entries.hint: The destruction of the Armenians was documented at the time by German missionaries (Johannes Lepsius, Deutschland und Armenien, 1919), by the British Blue Book of Bryce and Toynbee (1916), by American consuls and by Ambassador Morgenthau (1918), and by Ottoman court records of 1919–1920. Aram Andonian's 1920 'Memoirs of Naim Bey', with telegrams attributed to Talat, was long used as evidence but its authenticity is disputed. The Turkish state has regarded the western records as wartime propaganda.
entries.note: Bryce and Toynbee, The Treatment of Armenians in the Ottoman Empire (1916); Lepsius 1919; Henry Morgenthau, Ambassador Morgenthau's Story (1918); US National Archives RG 59 (867.4016); Andonian 1920; Dadrian and Akçam 2011.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The national economy policy, the abandoned property, the wartime famine and the Izmir congress

entries.label: The national economy policy
entries.hint: After 1913 the CUP government set out to create a 'national' Muslim-Turkish middle class: it protected new companies by the Law for the Encouragement of Industry, backed Muslim merchants, boycotts and cooperatives, and replaced foreign and Christian firms and staff. Historians such as Toprak, Akçam and Üngör argue that in the war years the removal of the Armenian and Greek economic role became an explicit aim. The programme was called the Millî İktisat.
entries.note: Zafer Toprak, Türkiye'de 'Millî İktisat' (1982); Law for the Encouragement of Industry (1913, 1915).

entries.label: The abandoned property
entries.hint: The land, houses, shops, churches, livestock and goods of the deported Armenians, valued in the millions of lira, were registered by liquidation commissions and sold or allotted to Muslim refugees, local notables, officials and institutions, with much simply seized. Few were returned after the war, and the Republic later had its own laws on the abandoned property, which the claims of survivors and their descendants still dispute.
entries.note: Emval-i metruke legislation (1915–1923); Üngör and Polatel 2011; Akçam and Kurt, The Spirit of the Laws (2015).

entries.label: The wartime famine
entries.hint: The conscription of men and draught animals, the requisition of grain, the cut-off of imports and a plague of locusts in 1915 reduced the harvests. Prices rose several times over; the countryside lacked labour; the cities of Anatolia suffered shortages and epidemic, though the worst famine in the empire fell on Mount Lebanon. Peasant households paid the main cost of the war.
entries.note: Yiğit Akın, When the War Came Home (2018); Mehmet Beşikçi, The Ottoman Mobilization of Manpower (2012); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The Izmir Economic Congress
entries.hint: Over two weeks in the burned city of Izmir in February and March 1923, about a thousand delegates of farmers, merchants, workers and industrialists met and, in the 'Misak-ı İktisadî', pledged a nationalist, private-enterprise economic programme: the development of national industry, abolition of the tithe and protection against foreign capital.
entries.note: Izmir İktisat Kongresi (1923) proceedings; Zürcher 1993; Zafer Toprak 1982.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The telegraph of the National Struggle and the tunnels of the Baghdad Railway

entries.label: The Taurus and Amanus tunnels
entries.hint: The last gaps in the Baghdad Railway, the tunnels through the Taurus and Amanus mountains, were driven with German engineers and the labour of deported Armenians, among others, and of prisoners; they were finished in 1918 as the war ended. Convoys of deportees passed along the line and its camps, and German railway staff reported on them.
entries.note: Baghdad Railway Company records (Deutsche Bank archive); Kévorkian 2011; Murat Özyüksel, The Berlin-Baghdad Railway (2014).

entries.label: The telegraph of the National Struggle
entries.hint: The Amasya Circular of 22 June 1919, which called the congress of Sivas and declared that the independence of the nation was in danger, was sent by telegraph from Amasya to the provincial governors and army commanders. Through the following months, Mustafa Kemal ran the movement from telegraph offices, often in night conversations with commanders; the post and telegraph staff and the lines were a key asset.
entries.note: Amasya Genelgesi (22 June 1919); Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, Nutuk (1927).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The German alliance, the refugees of the Balkan wars, the Soviet aid and the Khilafat funds

entries.label: The refugees from the Balkans
entries.hint: The Balkan wars drove hundreds of thousands of Muslims from Macedonia, Thrace and Bulgaria to Anatolia and the coast, and the Ottoman government settled them on abandoned Greek and Armenian lands and the sultan's domains. The refugees and their memories changed the politics of the officer class and the cities.
entries.note: Zürcher 2003; Kemal Karpat, Ottoman Population 1830–1914 (1985); Fuat Dündar, İttihat ve Terakki'nin Müslümanları İskân Politikası (2001).

entries.label: The German alliance
entries.hint: A secret treaty of alliance with Germany, signed on 2 August 1914 by the grand vizier Said Halim and the German ambassador, committed the Ottoman Empire to the German side if Russia entered the war. With the arrival of the warships Goeben and Breslau and the Black Sea raid of 29 October, the empire entered the war.
entries.note: Ottoman–German treaty (2 August 1914); Mustafa Aksakal, The Ottoman Road to War in 1914 (2008).

entries.label: The Khilafat movement
entries.hint: Indian Muslims in the Khilafat movement protested against the dismemberment of the Ottoman state and the caliph's position, and sent funds to the Anatolian movement and to the Red Crescent. When the Ankara assembly abolished the caliphate in 1924, the movement collapsed.
entries.note: Gail Minault, The Khilafat Movement (1982).

entries.label: The treaties of Moscow and Kars
entries.hint: The treaty of Moscow of 16 March 1921 between Ankara and Soviet Russia set the eastern border, left Batum to Georgia and brought Soviet gold, rifles and munitions to the national movement. The treaty of Kars on 13 October 1921 with the Soviet republics of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia confirmed the border in the east which is still in force.
entries.note: Treaty of Moscow (16 March 1921); Treaty of Kars (13 October 1921); Zürcher 1993.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The wartime partition plans, the American mandate question, the epidemics, the exchange of populations and the new demography

entries.label: The new demography of Anatolia
entries.hint: By Ottoman statistics, non-Muslims were roughly a fifth of the population of Anatolia in 1914, mostly Greeks and Armenians; the first census of the Republic in 1927 counted them as a few per cent of the whole. The change was the result of the genocide and deportation of the Armenians and Assyrians, the flight, killing and exchange of the Greeks, emigration, and the settlement of Muslim refugees.
entries.note: Karpat 1985; McCarthy 1983; Turkish census of 1927 (Genel Nüfus Sayımı); Zürcher 2003.

entries.label: The wartime partition agreements
entries.hint: The Allies agreed secretly in 1915 to give Russia Istanbul and the Straits, in the Sykes–Picot agreement of 1916 to divide the Arab provinces and south-eastern Anatolia between Britain and France, and in the agreement of St-Jean-de-Maurienne in 1917 to give Italy the south-west of Anatolia. The agreements were published by the Bolsheviks in November 1917, and shaped the Turkish memory of Sèvres.
entries.note: Constantinople agreement (March–April 1915); Sykes–Picot (May 1916); St-Jean-de-Maurienne (April 1917); David Fromkin, A Peace to End All Peace (1989).

entries.label: The influenza and typhus epidemics
entries.hint: Typhus, typhoid and relapsing fever swept through the army, the deportation convoys and the camps, and in 1918 the influenza pandemic reached Anatolia with the returning soldiers. Together with famine and war they contributed to a loss of life on the order of millions in these years, most of it from disease rather than combat; the totals are uncertain, and include the dead of the genocide.
entries.note: Hikmet Özdemir, The Ottoman Army 1914–1918 (2008); Justin McCarthy, Death and Exile (1995).

entries.label: The American mandate question
entries.hint: President Wilson was asked to take an American mandate over Armenia and the Straits: the King–Crane Commission (1919) and the Harbord Mission, which travelled in Anatolia in autumn 1919, studied the question, and in June 1920 the Senate refused. The refusal left the Armenian state without a guarantor.
entries.note: King–Crane Commission report (1919); Harbord report (October 1919); US Senate vote (1 June 1920); Hovannisian 1971–96.

entries.label: The evacuation of the White army
entries.hint: In November 1920, after the defeat of Wrangel in Crimea, some 130,000–150,000 soldiers and civilians were evacuated by sea to Istanbul and the surrounding coast, and were stranded in camps and in the city under the Allied occupation. Many moved on to Europe and the Balkans.
entries.note: Wrangel evacuation (13–16 November 1920); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The exchange of populations
entries.hint: The convention of 30 January 1923, signed at Lausanne, provided for the compulsory exchange of the Greek Orthodox of Turkey and the Muslims of Greece, with the exceptions of the Greeks of Istanbul and the Muslims of Western Thrace; the criterion was religion, not language. About 1.2 to 1.5 million Orthodox Christians left Anatolia, many of them already as refugees in 1922, and some 350,000 to 500,000 Muslims left Greece for Turkey. Many scholars describe it as a compulsory population transfer, and some as ethnic cleansing.
entries.note: Convention concerning the exchange of Greek and Turkish populations (30 January 1923); Renée Hirschon (ed.), Crossing the Aegean (2003); Bruce Clark, Twice a Stranger (2006).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Women's organisations and women at the front, the orphans of the deportations, the conscripts and the Karamanlides

entries.label: The women's organisations and press
entries.hint: After 1908 Ottoman women formed societies and journals of their own, among them the Teali-i Nisvan Cemiyeti (1908) and the Osmanlı Müdâfaa-i Hukuk-ı Nisvan Cemiyeti (1913), and the journal Kadınlar Dünyası (1913); in 1914 the Ottoman university opened a section for women. Halide Edib became the best-known woman writer, and in 1919–1922 took part in the national movement at the front.
entries.note: Serpil Çakır, Osmanlı Kadın Hareketi (1994); Halide Edib, The Turkish Ordeal (1928).

entries.label: The conscripts and deserters
entries.hint: About 2.8 million men were mobilised during the war, and many more soldiers died of disease and exposure than in battle. By 1917–1918 hundreds of thousands deserted, and in some districts the bands of deserters ruled the roads. The empire's war was borne by the Anatolian peasant.
entries.note: Beşikçi 2012; Erik Zürcher (ed.), Arming the State (1999); Özdemir 2008.

entries.label: The orphans and the converted
entries.hint: Tens of thousands of Armenian children and women, perhaps more, were taken into Muslim homes in 1915–1916 and brought up as Muslims, or were sold, married or adopted; some were later recovered, many were not, and in later years descendants have found the 'remnants of the sword' in their own families. The Near East Relief and the Allied commissions ran orphanages for those who were found.
entries.note: Near East Relief reports (1919–1923); Ara Sarafian (ed.), United States Official Documents; Ayşe Gül Altınay and Fethiye Çetin, Torunlar (2009).

entries.label: Women at the front
entries.hint: The supply of the Turkish army in the Greco-Turkish war depended on peasant women, who carried shells and food in ox-carts across the plateau to the front over winter roads while the men were at the front. Many of the individual stories told of them in later nationalist tradition cannot be verified.
entries.note: Beşikçi 2012; Zürcher 1993; Ottoman and Turkish war memoirs.

entries.label: The Karamanlides
entries.hint: The Turkish-speaking Orthodox Christians of Cappadocia, the Karamanlides, who wrote Turkish in Greek letters, were exchanged to Greece in 1923–1924 because of their religion, and there were taken as Greeks, speaking little Greek. Greek-speaking Muslims of Crete and Macedonia were settled in Anatolia on the same terms.
entries.note: Convention of 30 January 1923; Renée Hirschon 2003; Clark 2006.
